topics.title: Pattern overview
topics.summary: Singleton controls access to one instance while offering a shared way to obtain it. The attached chapter explicitly presents these as two linked decisions. A program may need one shared service while still benefiting from passing that service openly through parameters. Teaching this pattern includes recognizing its costs, not recommending it for every shared object.

blocks.title: Learning objectives
items: Implement one controlled instance with clear lifetime rules.
Distinguish once-only initialization from safe concurrent mutation.
Replace hidden global access with an injectable interface for isolated tests.

blocks.text: Restrict ordinary construction, prevent copying, and expose an accessor that repeatedly returns the same instance. The lifetime and concurrency rules depend on the implementation. Our function-local static is initialized once on first use; that language guarantee does not automatically protect later changes to the service. A separate lock must protect the ticket operation's shared mutable state.

cards.question: What is Singleton?
cards.answer: A design that controls access to one instance through a shared accessor.

cards.question: What is Mutex?
cards.answer: A synchronization object used to allow one participating thread at a time into a protected region.

cards.question: What is Critical section?
cards.answer: Code that accesses shared state while holding the required lock.

cards.question: What is Data race?
cards.answer: Unsynchronized conflicting accesses to memory by different threads, with at least one write; in C++ this causes undefined behavior.

cards.question: What is Dependency injection?
cards.answer: Supplying an object a component needs through an explicit parameter or constructor instead of locating it globally.

cards.question: Does a function-local static make next_++ thread-safe?
cards.answer: No. It protects initial construction, not later state changes. take must lock its exhaustion check and increment together.

cards.question: Why must a test not insist that the safe attached sample always prints FOO twice?
cards.answer: Either thread can initialize first. Both values must agree, but the language does not guarantee which input wins the race to acquire the lock.

topics.title: One dispenser, not one counter per caller
topics.summary: A small demonstration process issues tickets numbered 1, 2, and 3. Different callers must draw from the same sequence. After the third ticket, every request is rejected. Restarting the process starts a new sequence; the program does not store tickets on disk. This is a deliberately small model of a shared service, not a distributed ticket system.

blocks.text: The simplest good solution is often to create one ordinary dispenser in main and pass a reference to every user. That gives one instance by application arrangement. The excerpt shows a local counter’s core idea, assuming requests are sequential. If separate components each create their own counter, they can both issue ticket 1. Sharing one object is necessary for this requirement; global access is a separate design choice.

topics.title: What Singleton adds, and what it combines
topics.summary: The Singleton pattern controls construction so callers reach one instance through a shared access operation. TicketDispenser has a private constructor and destructor, deleted copy operations, and a static instance function returning a reference. Ordinary callers cannot create another object or copy the existing one. The function returns a reference because it lends the service; callers must not delete it.

blocks.text: Singleton combines two ideas: restricting instance count and providing global access. You may need the first without needing the second. Passing one ordinary object from main often expresses sharing more clearly, because function parameters reveal who depends on the service. We implement Singleton here to understand its exact mechanism and costs, then use the lab to remove hidden access from a consumer.

static on instance means the member function is called on the class rather than on an existing object. There is no this pointer for that call. The local static variable inside it has a different meaning: its storage lasts beyond one function call. It is initialized when execution first reaches its declaration and is reused on later calls. The returned references therefore all name the same completed dispenser in this program.

topics.title: Once-only initialization is not method synchronization
topics.summary: Since C++11, initialization of a function-local static is guarded so concurrent first callers do not each construct the object. One performs initialization while other callers wait for it to complete. If initialization throws, a later call can try again. Re-entering that same local static initialization recursively is not a safe way to resolve dependencies; avoid service constructors that cycle back through one another.

blocks.text: That guarantee concerns construction only. It does not protect later reads and writes to next_. Two threads incrementing an ordinary shared int without synchronization cause a data race and undefined behavior. It is not accurate to promise merely “one lost ticket”: the C++ program has no defined result for that race. Making the constructor private or the object global does not repair it.

The take operation uses a mutex, a lock that allows only one participating thread at a time into the protected region. lock_guard acquires gate_ when the guard is constructed and releases it when the guard leaves scope. Both the exhaustion check and the increment occur under that same lock. If the exception is thrown, stack cleanup still releases the lock. The local static guard and this method lock solve different problems and neither replaces the other.

The expression next_++ returns the old value and then increments the stored integer. The first three successful calls return 1, 2, and 3, leaving next_ equal to 4. Later calls test next_ > 3 and throw before incrementing again. The bounded sequence avoids overflow. Each whole take operation appears indivisible to other calls that use the same mutex. The standard does not promise fairness or which waiting caller gets a particular number.

topics.title: Lifetime and tests reveal the hidden coupling
topics.summary: The instance is destroyed during normal program shutdown if it was successfully initialized. Its private destructor prevents ordinary callers from explicitly destroying the borrowed object. In this single executable the accessor identifies one service. Separate processes have separate address spaces and separate instances; dynamic-library boundaries can also require careful linkage and deployment rules. Singleton is not a machine-wide lock, a distributed coordinator, or a persistence mechanism.

blocks.text: Shutdown dependencies deserve care. Another static object’s destructor must not use a service whose lifetime has already ended. A main-owned service with explicit lifetime often makes this ordering easier to see. Deliberately leaking a service to avoid shutdown ordering changes resource cleanup behavior and should never be an unexamined default.

Tests in one process share singleton state. A test that consumes ticket 1 changes what another test sees. Running the second test alone may pass while running the whole suite fails. A reset-for-tests method can hide the problem and may create races if used while work is active. This chapter’s main is a fresh-process demonstration with a known initial state. Its sequential checks verify identity, numbering, and repeated exhaustion; they are not a concurrency stress test.

The lab introduces TicketSource as the operation a consumer needs. admit accepts TicketSource& rather than finding the singleton itself. The production boundary can pass TicketDispenser::instance(), while each test can create a fresh LocalTickets. That technique is dependency injection: supplying a needed object explicitly. It preserves the option of one production instance while making tests independent.

topics.title: Choosing a shared service deliberately
topics.summary: A singleton can suit a truly process-wide service with a clear lifetime and little need for alternate instances. It is a poor fit when the program may run two independent sessions, load different configurations in tests, or need controlled startup and shutdown. Global access can make dependencies look smaller than they are because every function can silently acquire the service.

blocks.text: Do not replace every injected reference with a global accessor just to shorten parameter lists. Those parameters explain what the operation needs. Likewise, do not introduce an interface for every tiny value. TicketSource is justified in the lab by a concrete testing requirement: a consumer should work with independent counters as well as the shared production service.

For concurrency, one mutex protects only the state consistently accessed under it. If a future peek method reads next_ without locking, take’s lock does not make that new read safe. If two operations must form one transaction, locking each separately may still allow interleaving between them. Define the operation boundary first, then choose locking or an atomic design that preserves that boundary. Singleton answers where the object comes from; it does not answer every question about its correct use.

topics.title: Worked example: contracts and alternatives
topics.summary: A bounded process-wide ticket dispenser

blocks.title: Requirements
items: All accessor calls in this executable refer to one dispenser.
Issue exactly 1, 2, and 3, then reject every later request.
Protect the shared check-and-increment operation with one mutex.

blocks.text: A private constructor, deleted copying, and a local static instance control access and lifetime. A separate lock_guard protects mutable state during take. A reference lends the service without transferring ownership.

blocks.title: Invariants
items: Successful requests return distinct integers from 1 through 3.
next_ remains 4 after exhaustion; rejection does not consume more state.
Every mutable counter access in take occurs while gate_ is locked.

blocks.text: Alternative: Create one ordinary dispenser in main and pass references to its consumers. That keeps sharing explicit and makes independent instances easy to test. An interface is useful when consumers need both a shared production source and fresh test sources.

Verification: main checks that two references have the same address, checks tickets 1–3, and verifies repeated rejection after exhaustion. The code was compiled and executed with thread support. The supplied demonstration is sequential; it does not claim a stress test, fairness guarantee, or cross-process uniqueness.
Maintenance: Keep singleton access at a small application boundary. Pass the service or a narrow interface to ordinary code so tests and future multi-session uses can supply independent instances.

topics.title: Exercise 05.6: Justify a decision
topics.summary: A reviewer proposes a public reset() solely so tests can reuse the singleton. Explain a concrete risk and a better alternative for ordinary consumer tests.

blocks.title: Hint
blocks.text: Consider parallel tests or a live request during reset.

blocks.title: Explained answer
blocks.text: Reset can make ticket numbers repeat and can race with active requests unless a larger lifecycle policy exists. Fresh injected LocalTickets instances give each test a known starting state without changing production global state. A reset may be valid for a deliberately restartable service, but then it needs real domain semantics, synchronization, and tests rather than a hidden testing exception.

cards.question: A reviewer proposes a public reset() solely so tests can reuse the singleton. Explain a concrete risk and a better alternative for ordinary consumer tests.
cards.answer: Reset can make ticket numbers repeat and can race with active requests unless a larger lifecycle policy exists. Fresh injected LocalTickets instances give each test a known starting state without changing production global state. A reset may be valid for a deliberately restartable service, but then it needs real domain semantics, synchronization, and tests rather than a hidden testing exception.

blocks.title: Solution reasoning
blocks.text: LocalTickets owns the bounded counter and mutex. TicketDispenser owns one LocalTickets and delegates take. admit depends only on TicketSource. The solution therefore separates lifetime selection from ticket behavior and keeps tests independent. The local tests are sequential; additional concurrent tests could stress scheduling but would not replace the locking argument.

workshop.title: A bounded process-wide ticket dispenser
workshop.problem: A bounded process-wide ticket dispenser. All accessor calls in this executable refer to one dispenser. Issue exactly 1, 2, and 3, then reject every later request. Protect the shared check-and-increment operation with one mutex.
workshop.output:
same instance=yes
tickets=1,2,3
exhausted remains exhausted

steps.state: first and second refer to the same dispenser; next_=1
steps.why: The first accessor call initializes the local static; the second reuses it.
Each locked operation reads and increments one shared integer.
The exhaustion check occurs before incrementing.
Rejected operations leave the exhausted state unchanged.

workshop.pitfall: Assume local static initialization also synchronizes next_++. Concurrent calls without a method lock create a data race and undefined behavior. The once-only initialization guard protects construction, not later member accesses.

discussion.question: A server must support two independent customer sessions in one process, each starting at ticket 1. Choose Singleton or explicitly owned dispensers and explain the deciding requirement.
discussion.answer: Use one explicitly owned dispenser per session. Pass the appropriate reference to each consumer. A singleton would merge counters unless it became a more complex session registry, which is a different responsibility and unnecessary for this requirement.
discussion.hint: A process-wide instance combines both sessions’ state.

workshop.alternative: Create one ordinary dispenser in main and pass references to its consumers. That keeps sharing explicit and makes independent instances easy to test. An interface is useful when consumers need both a shared production source and fresh test sources.
workshop.design: A private constructor, deleted copying, and a local static instance control access and lifetime. A separate lock_guard protects mutable state during take. A reference lends the service without transferring ownership.
invariants: Successful requests return distinct integers from 1 through 3.
next_ remains 4 after exhaustion; rejection does not consume more state.
Every mutable counter access in take occurs while gate_ is locked.
workshop.maintenance: Keep singleton access at a small application boundary. Pass the service or a narrow interface to ordinary code so tests and future multi-session uses can supply independent instances.
workshop.verification: main checks that two references have the same address, checks tickets 1–3, and verifies repeated rejection after exhaustion. The code was compiled and executed with thread support. The supplied demonstration is sequential; it does not claim a stress test, fairness guarantee, or cross-process uniqueness.
